note: NestKeep task library. Costs are honest US approximations ('about'), never fake precision. frequencyMonths = how often the job repeats. seasons: spring, summer, fall, winter (empty = any).

needs: Replacement filter in the size printed on the old one
steps: Turn the system off at the thermostat.
Slide the old filter out and note its size and the airflow arrow direction.
Slide the new filter in with the arrow pointing toward the furnace.
Turn the system back on and write the date on the filter frame.
tasks.title: Change the HVAC air filter
tasks.why: A clogged filter makes the system work harder, raises the power bill and shortens the life of the blower motor.

steps: Switch the outdoor unit off at the disconnect box.
Clear leaves and debris from around the unit, keeping 2 feet of space.
Spray the coils gently from inside out with a garden hose, never a pressure washer.
Straighten any badly bent fins with a fin comb.
Restore power and check cool air at a vent.
tasks.title: Clean the AC condenser coils
tasks.why: Dirt and cottonwood fluff on the outdoor coils can cut cooling efficiency by a fifth and overheat the compressor.

steps: Call your HVAC company before the first cold snap, when prices and waits are lowest.
Ask for a combustion check and heat exchanger inspection in writing.
Keep the service report with your home records.
tasks.title: Book the annual furnace service
tasks.why: A yearly service catches a cracked heat exchanger, which can leak carbon monoxide, before heating season starts.

steps: Book before the first hot week of the year.
Ask for refrigerant level, capacitor and drain line checks.
Keep the report with your home records.
tasks.title: Book the annual AC service
tasks.why: Low refrigerant and worn capacitors are cheap in spring and an emergency callout in the first heatwave.

steps: Find the PVC drain line near the indoor unit.
Pour a cup of white vinegar into the access tee.
Check the outside drain end is dripping freely.
If blocked, clear it with a wet/dry vacuum from outside.
tasks.title: Flush the AC condensate drain
tasks.why: A clogged condensate line backs water into the ceiling or the furnace closet, and the damage is always worse than the flush.

needs: Batteries in the size your thermostat takes
steps: Replace the batteries even if it still lights up.
Run the heat and the AC for two minutes each to confirm both respond.
Check the programmed schedule still matches your routine.
tasks.title: Check the thermostat and its batteries
tasks.why: Dead thermostat batteries on the coldest night means no heat and a possible frozen pipe bill.

steps: Turn the humidifier control off and close its water valve.
Open the cover on the furnace-mounted unit.
Swap the pad, checking the water feed tube is clear.
Restore water and power and set humidity to about 35 percent.
tasks.title: Replace the humidifier pad
tasks.why: A scaled-up pad stops humidifying and can grow mould that the furnace then blows through the whole house.

steps: Turn off power (breaker) or set gas to pilot, and close the cold inlet.
Attach a hose to the drain valve and run it to a floor drain.
Open the drain and a hot tap upstairs until the water runs clear.
Close everything, refill fully, then restore power or gas.
tasks.title: Flush the water heater
tasks.why: Sediment at the bottom of the tank cooks the element or the burner and is the main reason water heaters die young.

steps: Turn off power or gas and the cold inlet, and drain a few gallons.
Unscrew the rod from the top of the tank with a socket wrench.
If it is mostly eaten away or coated in calcium, replace it.
Refill the tank before restoring power.
tasks.title: Check the water heater anode rod
tasks.why: The anode rod rusts so your tank does not. When it is eaten through, the tank itself starts rusting and leaks follow.

steps: Pour a bucket of water slowly into the pit.
The float should rise and the pump should kick on and clear the water.
Check the discharge line outside is not blocked or frozen.
If it hums but does not pump, it needs replacing before storm season.
tasks.title: Test the sump pump
tasks.why: A sump pump that died silently in winter announces itself during the first spring storm, through your basement floor.

steps: Empty each under-sink cabinet.
Run the tap and the drain, then feel every pipe joint and supply line with a dry hand or tissue.
Check for water stains, swelling or a musty smell.
Tighten or re-seat anything that weeps, or book a plumber if a joint is corroded.
tasks.title: Check under every sink for leaks
tasks.why: A slow drip under a sink rots the cabinet floor and the subfloor for months before anyone notices.

steps: Unscrew the aerator from each tap by hand or with pliers and a cloth.
Rinse the screens, and soak them in vinegar for an hour if scaled.
Rinse, refit, and check flow.
tasks.title: Clean the faucet aerators
tasks.why: Grit and scale in aerators strangle water flow and make a good tap feel like a plumbing problem.

steps: Disconnect and drain all garden hoses and store them inside.
Close the inside shutoff for each outdoor faucet, then open the outside tap to drain it.
Fit foam faucet covers outside.
tasks.title: Winterize outdoor faucets and hoses
tasks.why: Water left in an outdoor line freezes, splits the pipe inside the wall, and you find out in spring when you turn it on.

steps: Put a few drops of food colouring in the tank and wait 20 minutes without flushing.
If colour appears in the bowl, the flapper is leaking.
Replace the flapper, they are cheap and tool-free on most toilets.
Check the water level sits about an inch below the overflow tube.
tasks.title: Check toilet flappers and fill valves
tasks.why: A silently leaking toilet can waste hundreds of gallons a day and is one of the most common surprise water bills.

steps: Run cold water and feed in a tray of ice cubes to scour the plates.
Follow with half a lemon cut in pieces.
Never reach inside with your hand, use tongs for anything dropped in.
tasks.title: Clean the garbage disposal
tasks.why: Old food film inside the disposal is the usual source of the mystery kitchen smell.

steps: Find the main shutoff (basement, garage or meter box).
Close it fully, open a tap to confirm the water stops, then reopen it.
Make sure everyone in the house knows where it is.
tasks.title: Exercise the main water shutoff valve
tasks.why: The day a pipe bursts is the wrong day to discover the shutoff valve has seized solid.

steps: Scoop debris into a bucket, working from a stable ladder with someone footing it.
Flush each run with a hose and watch for leaks at joints.
Check downspouts run freely and splash blocks push water away from the house.
Consider guards only if trees overhang heavily, they reduce, not remove, this job.
tasks.title: Clean the gutters and downspouts
tasks.why: Overflowing gutters pour water down your walls and into the foundation, the most expensive place water can go.

steps: Walk the perimeter with binoculars and look for missing, curled or lifted shingles.
Check flashing around chimneys and vents for gaps or rust.
Look in the attic for daylight, stains or damp insulation after rain.
Book a roofer for anything beyond a single shingle.
tasks.title: Inspect the roof from the ground
tasks.why: One lifted or missing shingle is a cheap repair; the same leak left a year is rotten decking and a ceiling stain.

steps: Measure insulation depth; about 10 to 14 inches is typical for cold climates.
Check vents are not blocked by insulation or stored boxes.
Look for mould, damp patches or daylight at the edges.
tasks.title: Check attic insulation and ventilation
tasks.why: Thin or damp attic insulation means heat escaping all winter and ice dams forming on the roof edge.

steps: Cut back anything touching or within about 6 feet of the roof.
Never work near power lines; that is a utility or tree-service job.
Clear what fell into the gutters while you are there.
tasks.title: Trim branches away from the roof
tasks.why: Branches rubbing the roof strip the shingle surface, and a storm turns an overhanging limb into a roof repair.

steps: Walk the outside and mark every cracked or separated joint.
Cut out failed caulk, wipe the joint dry.
Run a fresh bead, smooth it with a wet finger, and let it cure before rain.
tasks.title: Re-caulk windows and door frames
tasks.why: Cracked exterior caulk is an open door for water and cold air, and it fails quietly a joint at a time.

steps: Sweep cracks clean and let the surface dry fully.
Fill cracks with crack filler, larger ones with backer rod first.
Consider a full seal coat every 2 to 3 years on asphalt.
tasks.title: Seal driveway cracks
tasks.why: Water in a small crack freezes, widens it all winter, and turns a tube of filler into a resurfacing bill.

steps: Use a garden hose and soft brush with house wash, working bottom to top, rinsing top down.
Avoid pressure washers on wood, fibre cement and older vinyl; they force water behind the boards.
Check for soft or bubbling paint while you wash and note it for touch-up.
tasks.title: Wash the siding
tasks.why: Algae and grime hold moisture against siding and paint, and a gentle wash adds years to both.

steps: Push a screwdriver into boards near the ground and posts; soft means rot has started.
Tighten loose boards and hammer down lifted nails, or swap to screws.
Clean, let dry two good days, then apply sealer or stain.
tasks.title: Check and seal the deck
tasks.why: A deck board that fails the screwdriver test this year is a replaced deck in five; sealer is the cheap version of that story.

steps: Lubricate rollers, hinges and springs with garage-door spray (not grease).
Test balance: disconnect the opener and lift the door halfway; it should stay put.
Test the auto-reverse with a block of wood on the floor; it must reverse on contact.
Tighten the visible hinge bolts.
tasks.title: Service the garage door
tasks.why: A door that is out of balance makes the opener strain on every cycle until the gear or the spring gives up.

steps: Open the water supply slowly and fill the main line.
Run each zone and walk it: look for geysers, tilted heads and dry arcs.
Adjust or replace broken heads and note the controller schedule.
tasks.title: Start up the sprinkler system
tasks.why: A head cracked by winter ice sprays your foundation or the street all summer before anyone notices.

needs: Irrigation company or an air compressor
steps: Close the sprinkler water supply and open the drains.
Either book a blow-out service or use a compressor zone by zone at safe pressure.
Leave valves half open for winter.
tasks.title: Blow out the sprinkler system
tasks.why: Water left in sprinkler lines freezes and splits pipes underground, where every repair starts with digging.

steps: Unplug the fridge or switch it off.
Pull the bottom grille or rear panel and vacuum the coils with a brush attachment.
A long coil brush reaches what the vacuum misses.
Restore power and check it cycles off normally.
tasks.title: Clean the refrigerator coils
tasks.why: Dust-blanketed coils make the fridge run hot and long, and the compressor pays for it.

steps: Twist out the old filter (inside the fridge or in the grille).
Fit the new one and run two litres of water through the dispenser to flush it.
Reset the filter light.
tasks.title: Replace the fridge water filter
tasks.why: An exhausted filter stops filtering long before the light comes on, and flow slows to a trickle.

steps: Twist out the filter at the bottom and wash it in hot soapy water.
Check the spray arm holes for seeds and glass slivers.
Run the hottest empty cycle with a cup of vinegar in a bowl on the top rack.
tasks.title: Clean the dishwasher filter and arms
tasks.why: A clogged filter is why dishes come out gritty, and it strains the drain pump on every cycle.

steps: Wipe the door gasket folds and leave the door ajar after washes.
Run an empty hot cycle with a machine cleaner or vinegar.
Feel both supply hoses for bulges or cracks; replace rubber hoses every 5 years, braided steel lasts longer.
tasks.title: Clean the washing machine and check hoses
tasks.why: A burst rubber washer hose is one of the top causes of home water damage, and the mould smell comes free with a dirty gasket.

steps: Slide or unclip the metal filter.
Soak it in hot water with degreasing dish soap for 15 minutes and scrub.
Dry fully before refitting.
tasks.title: Clean the range hood filter
tasks.why: A grease-loaded filter stops catching grease, which then coats the kitchen and becomes a fire risk above the stove.

steps: Look for gaps, black mould that will not scrub off, or caulk pulling away.
Cut out failed sections, clean with bleach solution, let dry fully.
Run a fresh bead of kitchen-and-bath caulk and smooth it.
tasks.title: Check bathroom caulk and grout
tasks.why: Failed caulk behind a tub lets water into the wall on every shower, and walls rot silently for years.

steps: Press TEST on each kitchen, bathroom, garage and outdoor outlet; power should cut.
Press RESET to restore it.
Replace any outlet that will not trip or will not reset.
tasks.title: Test GFCI outlets
tasks.why: A GFCI that no longer trips is just an outlet, usually discovered after it mattered.

steps: Press the test button on every smoke and carbon monoxide alarm.
Replace batteries in any that sound weak, even if they pass.
Vacuum dust off the vents while you are up there.
tasks.title: Test smoke and CO alarms
tasks.why: Alarms only protect you if they work; most fire deaths happen in homes with no working smoke alarm.

needs: New alarms for any that are expired
steps: Check the manufacture date printed on each alarm.
Replace smoke alarms over 10 years old and CO alarms over 7.
Write the install date on the new alarm with a marker.
tasks.title: Replace out-of-date alarms
tasks.why: Smoke alarm sensors wear out: at 10 years old (7 for CO) the alarm can look fine and still fail to sense.

steps: Pull the dryer out and disconnect the vent hose.
Brush the full line with a vent brush kit, including the outside hood.
Vacuum the lint trap housing and check the outside flap opens when running.
Reconnect with metal tape, never screws that catch lint.
tasks.title: Clean the dryer vent line
tasks.why: Lint packed in the vent line is a leading cause of house fires, and it doubles drying time long before that.

steps: Check the pressure gauge sits in the green.
Look for rust, a cracked hose or a missing pin.
Shake dry-chemical extinguishers to keep the powder loose.
Replace or recharge anything out of date; keep one in the kitchen and one near bedrooms.
tasks.title: Check fire extinguishers
tasks.why: An extinguisher with a flat gauge is decoration. The check takes a minute a year.

steps: Place a test kit in the lowest lived-in level, away from drafts.
Leave it for the stated period (usually 2 to 4 days) with windows closed.
Mail it to the lab; if results are at or above 4 pCi/L, get a mitigation quote.
tasks.title: Test for radon
tasks.why: Radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer and is common in many US regions; you cannot see or smell it, only test for it.

steps: Pop off the return grilles and vacuum inside as far as the hose reaches.
Wash grilles in soapy water and dry before refitting.
Check no supply vent is blocked by furniture or rugs.
tasks.title: Vacuum vents and returns
tasks.why: Dust-choked returns starve the system of air and spread dust through every room each cycle.

steps: Walk the attic, basement or crawlspace with the system running.
Feel along joints for moving air.
Seal gaps with mastic or metal tape, never cloth duct tape.
Note crushed or disconnected runs for a pro if you cannot reach them.
tasks.title: Inspect visible ductwork
tasks.why: Leaking ducts in an attic or crawlspace can lose a quarter of the air you paid to heat or cool.

steps: Open the brine tank and check the salt level sits above the water.
Break up any hard salt crust bridging the top.
Top up with the salt type your manual specifies.
tasks.title: Check water softener salt
tasks.why: An empty brine tank means hard water quietly scaling the water heater, dishwasher and every tap.

steps: Put a bucket under the discharge pipe.
Lift the valve lever briefly; hot water should flow, then stop cleanly when released.
If it will not open or keeps dripping, replace the valve or call a plumber.
tasks.title: Test the water heater T&P valve
tasks.why: The temperature-and-pressure relief valve is the safety device that stops a water heater becoming a pressure bomb; it seizes if never tested.

steps: Tie a bag of white vinegar over the showerhead so it is submerged.
Leave overnight, remove, and scrub the nozzles with an old toothbrush.
Run the shower for a minute to flush.
tasks.title: Descale showerheads
tasks.why: Mineral scale turns a good shower into a sideways spray and strains the mixer cartridge.

steps: Remove the stopper and pull out hair and soap build-up with a drain tool.
Flush with a kettle of hot water.
Fit strainers on bathroom drains to slow the next build-up.
tasks.title: Clear slow drains properly
tasks.why: A slow drain is a blockage announcing itself; chemical openers damage pipes and rarely fix the hair and grease causing it.

steps: From the ground with binoculars, confirm the cap is present and straight.
Check the flashing line where chimney meets roof for gaps.
Look at the mortar for crumbling joints and book tuckpointing if it is powdering.
tasks.title: Check chimney cap and flashing
tasks.why: A missing chimney cap lets rain and animals straight into the flue, and failed flashing is a classic hidden leak.

steps: Apply a roof-safe moss treatment from the ladder edge or with an extended sprayer; never pressure wash shingles.
Let weather wash the dead moss off over the following weeks.
Trim the worst overhanging shade if it keeps returning.
tasks.title: Treat roof moss and algae
tasks.why: Moss lifts shingle edges and holds water against the roof, halving the life of the shaded side.

steps: Walk the full perimeter and check the ground slopes away from the walls.
Mark cracks wider than a coin's thickness and photograph them with a date for comparison.
Clear soil and mulch a few inches below siding and vents.
Add soil to low spots so water runs away, not in.
tasks.title: Walk the foundation
tasks.why: Soil that slopes toward the house and cracks at the base are the earliest, cheapest warnings of foundation trouble.

steps: Scrape anything loose or blistering back to sound wood.
Sand, prime bare spots, and let the primer dry.
Match the existing paint and feather two thin coats.
tasks.title: Touch up failing paint
tasks.why: Paint is the waterproof skin of wood siding and trim; one blistered board left bare rots in a single wet season.

steps: Open every window and inspect the screen mesh for tears.
Patch small holes or re-screen the frame with a spline roller.
Check for fog between double panes, a sign the seal has failed.
Lubricate sticking window tracks with silicone spray.
tasks.title: Check window screens and seals
tasks.why: Torn screens invite insects all summer, and failed window seals show up as fogged glass and lost insulation.

steps: Puff graphite powder into each exterior lock, never oil, which traps grit.
Work the key in and out a few times.
Oil squeaking door hinges with a drop of light oil and wipe the excess.
tasks.title: Lubricate locks and hinges
tasks.why: A lock that needs force is wearing its key and itself out; graphite keeps it smooth without gumming it up.

steps: Push each post at ground level; any that rock need bracing or resetting.
Check boards and rails for rot at the bottom edge with a screwdriver.
Oil gate hinges and confirm latches catch on their own.
tasks.title: Check fences and gates
tasks.why: One leaning post ignored becomes a fence line replaced after the first storm flattens it.

steps: Switch the fan off at the breaker if you will remove the cover.
Pull the cover down, wash it, and vacuum the fan blades and housing.
Hold a tissue near the running fan; it should pull it firmly to the grille.
tasks.title: Clean bathroom exhaust fans
tasks.why: A dust-choked fan moves almost no air, so shower steam stays in the room and feeds mould on the ceiling.

steps: Pour a bucket of water slowly into each basement or laundry floor drain.
Add a teaspoon of cooking oil on top to slow evaporation.
Note any drain that gurgles or backs up for a plumber visit.
tasks.title: Top up floor drain traps
tasks.why: A dry floor-drain trap is an open pipe to the sewer, and the smell arrives long before anyone connects the two.

steps: Slip a pillowcase over each blade and pull the dust off into it.
Flip the direction switch on the motor: counter-clockwise for summer, clockwise on low for winter.
Check the fan runs without wobble on high.
tasks.title: Clean and reverse ceiling fans
tasks.why: Fans should push air down in summer and pull it up in winter; dust-heavy blades do neither well and shower the room.

steps: Leave an appliance thermometer in a glass of water in the fridge overnight.
Fridge should read 37 to 40°F, freezer 0°F or below.
Adjust one notch at a time and re-check the next day.
Check door seals grip a banknote all the way round; a loose seal leaks cold air.
tasks.title: Check fridge and freezer temperatures
tasks.why: A fridge drifting above 40°F spoils food quietly, and a freezer above 0°F shortens the life of everything in it.

steps: Test each sensor by touching its contacts with a damp finger; it should sound or alert.
Replace batteries in any that are weak.
Confirm sensors sit under the water heater, washer, fridge line and sinks.
tasks.title: Check leak sensors and batteries
tasks.why: A leak sensor with a flat battery is silent during the exact slow leak it was bought to catch.

steps: Slide the filter out from under the microwave.
Soak in hot water with degreasing dish soap, scrub, and dry.
Replace charcoal filters instead of washing them, about every 6 months.
tasks.title: Clean the microwave grease filter
tasks.why: On over-range microwaves the grease filter protects the fan; a blocked one vents steam back into the kitchen.

steps: Empty and wash the bucket with a mild bleach solution.
Rinse the air filter and let it dry fully.
Vacuum the coils gently and set humidity to about 45 percent.
tasks.title: Clean the dehumidifier
tasks.why: A clogged dehumidifier filter makes the unit run constantly while the basement stays damp enough for mould.

steps: Vacuum washable pre-filters monthly and let them dry.
Replace HEPA and carbon filters at the interval on the filter itself.
Reset the filter indicator after changing.
tasks.title: Replace purifier and vacuum filters
tasks.why: A spent HEPA filter stops cleaning the air while the machine still sounds like it is working.

steps: Run a banknote around the closed door; it should grip evenly.
Clean the gasket with warm soapy water to remove baked-on grease.
Replace the gasket if it is cracked, flattened or loose in sections.
tasks.title: Check the oven door seal
tasks.why: A perished oven gasket leaks heat on every bake, stretching cooking times and heating the kitchen instead of the food.

steps: Inspect cords and plugs for damage before first use.
Place heaters on a hard flat surface, a metre from bedding, curtains and furniture.
Confirm the tip-over switch cuts power when lifted.
Never run one on an extension cord or overnight unattended.
tasks.title: Space heater safety check
tasks.why: Space heaters cause a large share of winter house fires, almost always through placement or a damaged cord.

steps: Brush soapy water on gas hoses and connections and open the tank; bubbles mean a leak.
Clear burner tubes and check for rust-through.
Scrub grates, empty the grease tray, and test every burner lights evenly.
tasks.title: Check the grill before season
tasks.why: A cracked gas hose or a spider nest in a burner tube is how the first barbecue of the year becomes a fire call.

needs: Replacement water or food if expired
steps: Test every torch and replace batteries; keep spares with it.
Check stored water and tinned food dates and rotate anything expiring.
Charge the power bank and confirm the phone car charger is in the car.
Make sure the kit includes the house shutoff wrench if your meter needs one.
tasks.title: Refresh the storm kit
tasks.why: Torches with dead batteries and expired water are the standard state of a storm kit that is never checked.

steps: Clean the filter and let the unit dry fully on fan mode.
Either remove and store it inside, or fit an insulated exterior cover.
Seal gaps around the unit with foam strips if it stays in.
tasks.title: Store or cover window AC units
tasks.why: A window unit left bare all winter leaks cold air around it and rusts its coils with trapped moisture.

steps: Walk everyone in the house to the main water shutoff and the breaker panel.
Tag both with bright labels.
Save a photo of each location in the app for the babysitter-and-guests moments.
tasks.title: Show everyone the shutoffs
tasks.why: In a burst-pipe emergency the water stops when someone who is home knows the valve, not when the one who knows lands.

steps: Fit a pressure gauge to an outside tap or laundry tap.
Turn off all water use, open that tap fully and read the gauge.
Healthy is 40 to 80 psi; above that, a plumber should check the regulator.
tasks.title: Check home water pressure
tasks.why: Pressure above 80 psi quietly destroys appliance valves, hoses and water heater life; too low often means a failing regulator.

steps: Run the dryer and check the outside flap opens fully with strong airflow.
Clear any screen or guard that catches lint; vent hoods should not be screened.
Clear shrubs or mulch blocking the outlet.
tasks.title: Check the dryer vent outlet
tasks.why: A vent hood stuck shut or screened over traps moist air and lint, whatever you cleaned inside.

steps: Look for droppings, nests, chewed wires and disturbed insulation.
Check vents and eaves for gaps bigger than a coin.
Seal gaps with mesh or foam; call pest control for an active nest.
tasks.title: Check attic and crawlspace for pests
tasks.why: Droppings, chewed insulation and new daylight holes in autumn mean animals are moving in for winter.

steps: Vacuum dust from the cabinet exterior, vents and the floor around the unit.
Move anything stored within a metre of the furnace, especially paint and solvents.
Check the area around the flue pipe is clear and dry.
tasks.title: Deep clean the furnace area
tasks.why: Dust and stored clutter around the furnace feed the blower and are a fire load next to a flame appliance.

steps: Inspect every string for cracked insulation, bare wire or broken sockets and bin the bad ones.
Use outdoor-rated cords and lights outside, and keep connections off the ground.
Do not chain more sets than the packaging allows; use a timer instead of all-night running.
tasks.title: Check holiday lights and cords
tasks.why: Frayed light strings and overloaded extension cords are a December staple for fire crews.

steps: Run each outdoor tap and watch the breaker cap for spraying.
Replace any breaker that sprays, drips constantly or is missing.
Confirm frost-free taps drain when shut off.
tasks.title: Check hose bib vacuum breakers
tasks.why: A failed vacuum breaker can siphon garden water back into the drinking supply, and a split one sprays every time the tap opens.

steps: Confirm there is a smoke alarm inside every bedroom, outside each sleeping area, and on every level.
Add alarms where any are missing; interconnected models alert the whole house.
Confirm a CO alarm sits near sleeping areas if the home has fuel appliances or a garage.
tasks.title: Check alarm placement coverage
tasks.why: Alarms only in hallways miss the bedrooms where most fatal fires start; coverage, not count, is what protects sleepers.

steps: Turn the pump off at the timer or switch.
Empty the skimmer and pump baskets of leaves and debris.
Remove the filter and rinse it top to bottom with a garden hose, working between the pleats on cartridge filters.
Soak heavily soiled cartridges overnight in filter cleaner, then rinse again.
Reassemble, turn the pump on, and note the clean pressure reading; a rise of 8 to 10 psi over this number is your next cleaning signal.
tasks.title: Clean the pool filter and pump basket
tasks.why: A clogged filter strains the pump, clouds the water and lets algae take hold. Pumps are one of the priciest parts of a pool to replace.

needs: Test strips or a liquid test kit
Chlorine and pH adjusters as needed
steps: Dip a test strip or take a sample elbow-deep, away from the jets.
Check chlorine (aim 1 to 3 ppm) and pH (aim 7.2 to 7.6).
Adjust one chemical at a time, run the pump for an hour, then retest.
For a hot tub, also check the waterline and filter rinse weekly in heavy use months.
tasks.title: Test and balance pool or hot tub water
tasks.why: Unbalanced water eats heaters, pumps and liners, and grows bacteria fast in warm water. Five minutes of testing prevents most of it.

steps: Find your last pumping record; most tanks need pumping every 3 to 5 years depending on household size.
Book a licensed septic service and ask them to inspect the baffles and effluent filter while the tank is open.
Keep the receipt and note the date and the sludge level they report; it sets your next interval.
Until the next pump: spread laundry across the week and keep grease, wipes and chemicals out of drains.
tasks.title: Pump the septic tank
tasks.why: A full tank pushes solids into the drain field, and a failed drain field is one of the most expensive repairs a home can need. Pumping is cheap insurance.

needs: A state-certified lab test kit (often from your county health office)
steps: Order a test kit from a certified lab or your county health office.
Run the cold tap for several minutes, then collect the sample exactly as the kit directs, without touching the inside of the bottle.
Mail or drop off the sample the same day; labs test for coliform bacteria and nitrates at minimum.
Keep the report with your home records and retest sooner after any flood, well work, or change in taste or smell.
tasks.title: Test well water for bacteria and nitrates
tasks.why: Well water is unregulated: nobody tests it but you. Annual testing catches bacterial contamination and rising nitrates before they become a health problem.

needs: Replacement sediment filter cartridge in your housing size
Filter wrench (usually supplied with the housing)
steps: Shut off the water before the filter housing and open a nearby tap to release pressure.
Unscrew the housing with the filter wrench and slide the old cartridge out.
Rinse the housing, check the O-ring and lightly grease it if it looks dry.
Fit the new cartridge, tighten the housing hand-tight plus a quarter turn, and restore water slowly, checking for drips.
tasks.title: Replace the well sediment filter
tasks.why: A clogged sediment filter drops water pressure through the whole house and lets grit reach pumps, softeners and appliances.

needs: Soft brush or squeegee on a pole
steps: Work early in the morning when panels are cool; never spray cold water on hot panels.
From the ground or a stable ladder position, rinse panels with a garden hose; never pressure wash.
Wash stubborn dirt with a soft brush and plain water or a little mild soap, then rinse.
While you are looking: check for cracked glass, loose mounts, chewed cables and new shading from growing trees. Compare this month's output in your inverter app with the same month last year.
tasks.title: Clean and inspect solar panels
tasks.why: Dust, pollen and bird droppings quietly cut panel output, often by 10 percent or more. Cleaning twice a year keeps the system earning what it should.

steps: Start the generator and let it run for 10 to 15 minutes; many models self-test weekly, this confirms it under your eye.
If it can carry load safely, let it power part of the house briefly and listen for surging or rough running.
Check oil level, look for leaks, and clear leaves or nests from the enclosure and exhaust.
Note the run hours from the meter; service intervals are based on them.
tasks.title: Run the standby generator under load
tasks.why: Generators fail silently in the months nobody needs them, then fail loudly during the outage they were bought for. A short monthly run keeps seals wet, batteries charged and problems visible.

needs: Engine oil and filter for your model
steps: With the generator off and cool, change the oil and oil filter.
Replace the spark plug and air filter, or clean them if your manual allows.
Check battery terminals for corrosion and top up the fuel stabilizer if it runs on stored fuel.
Run it for five minutes, confirm clean startup and no warning lights, and log the service date and run hours.
tasks.title: Service the standby generator
tasks.why: Oil, plugs and filters are the whole life of a small standby engine. One service a year, before storm and freeze season, is what makes it start on the one night it matters.

steps: Unplug the connector and look over the whole cable for cuts, kinks, crushed spots or scorch marks.
Check the connector pins are clean and straight, and wipe the handle with a dry cloth.
Press the charger's test button if it has one (GFCI test), then reset it and confirm the status light returns to normal.
Look and feel for heat damage: a plug or outlet that is warm after charging, or smells of hot plastic, means stop and call an electrician.
Coil the cable loosely and holster the connector so it stays dry and off the ground.
tasks.title: Inspect the EV charger and cable
tasks.why: The cable and connector take daily wear, weather and heat cycles. A damaged cable or a hot connection is a fire risk and can take the charger, or the car's charge port, with it.

needs: The charger's phone app (if it has one)
A licensed electrician if anything looks heat-damaged
steps: Switch the charger off at the breaker before cleaning anything.
Wipe the housing and connector with a dry cloth; clean the contacts only the way the manual allows, never with water.
Check the wall mount is tight and the cable's strain relief is not pulling loose.
Turn the power back on and check the charger's app for firmware updates; install any waiting.
If terminals, the plug or the outlet show any heat discolouration, book a licensed electrician for a torque and connection check instead of charging on.
tasks.title: Deep clean the EV charger and check for updates
tasks.why: Connections loosen and corrode over a year of daily charging, and loose connections are what overheat. Firmware updates fix charging faults and safety issues the maker has found since install.
